query: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr exhibits 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility in the cast state and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C at strain rates of 10−4–10−2 s−1, but inadequate oxygen resistance prevents most practical high-temperature applications. Earlier oxidation-protection research prevented pesting in a related, non-equiatomic Hf–Nb–Ta–Ti–Zr alloy during a 5 h exposure to air at 800 °C, but that result does not establish protection for equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr; related studies on other refractory alloys likewise did not evaluate this composition. With preservation of useful room- and high-temperature mechanical performance as a design constraint, what single intervention could improve the oxygen resistance of equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr? Formulate one hypothesis identifying the intervention and mechanism, predicting the outcome relative to untreated material, defining the applicable temperature, atmosphere, exposure-time, and loading boundaries, citing supporting evidence from the prior studies, and specifying a controlled experiment and result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A trace addition (around 1–3 atomic %) of tin (Sn) to equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr will improve its oxygen resistance by promoting the formation of a protective, adherent oxide scale that suppresses pest oxidation while preserving its existing room‐ and high‐temperature mechanical properties.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr with 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C.
generation.intervention: Incorporate a small Sn content (e.g., 1–3 at.% relative to the total composition) during alloy synthesis.
generation.conditions: Exposure in air at approximately 800 °C for durations around 5 hours, with testing under similar strain-rate conditions (10^(-4)–10^(-2) s⁻¹) used for mechanical evaluations.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a Sn-enriched subscale at grain boundaries and near the surface that acts as an oxygen diffusion barrier.
generation.mechanism: Tin, as a reactive element, can promote the formation of a dense, adherent oxide scale that retards oxygen penetration (and hence pest oxidation) by lowering oxygen diffusivity along grain boundaries. This selective oxidation does not significantly disrupt the microstructural features responsible for the alloy’s mechanical performance.
generation.predicted_outcome: The Sn-doped alloy will exhibit a marked reduction or delay of pest oxidation (evidenced by lower mass loss and improved oxide scale integrity) while maintaining similar room-temperature ductility (8–16%) and high-temperature yield strength (163–530 MPa) compared to the untreated alloy.
generation.baseline: Untreated equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr displays inadequate oxygen resistance with evidence of pest oxidation under similar test conditions.
generation.boundary: Effective in air at 800 °C for at least 5 hours; the intervention is designed to be compatible with the cast state of the alloy without additional coatings or extensive post-treatment, though the precise Sn level and long-term stability require further optimization.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal Sn content and its long-term effects on microstructure evolution and mechanical properties remain to be fully characterized. There is also some uncertainty about any potential subtle changes in ductility or strength under prolonged exposure conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one batch of equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr with 1–3 at.% Sn addition and one batch of the undoped (control) alloy. Expose both sets to air at 800 °C for 5 hours. Post-exposure, characterize the oxidation scale using SEM/EDS to assess its continuity and adherence and measure mass loss. Then perform standard tensile tests at room temperature and high-temperature tests (around 1000 °C) to compare mechanical properties.
measurements: Morphology and adhesion of the oxide scale (via SEM/EDS)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Sn-doped samples do not show statistically significant improvement in oxidation resistance (e.g., similar or higher mass loss, evidence of pest oxidation, poor oxide scale adherence) or if their mechanical properties (ductility and yield strength) fall outside the acceptable range compared to the control, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Structural metallic materials for applications at high temperatures must have a balance of mechanical properties and oxidation resistance. Coated and internally cooled Ni-based superalloys are used in gas turbine engines close to their high temperature limit, which is imposed by the melting temperature of Ni. The search for new alloys with similar or better capabilities at higher temperatures has concentrated on Nb-silicide based alloys that have lower densities, significantly higher solidus temperatures in excess of 1900 °C and can offer notable mechanical properties []. For example, some of these alloys can have compressive yield strength of about 1800 MPa at room temperature, 1200 MPa at 1000 °C and 500 MPa at 1200 °C []. The oxidation resistance of Nb-silicide based alloys was improved dramatically when the key alloying elements Al, Cr, Si, and Ti were in synergy with other transition and refractory metals, for example Hf, Mo, and simple metal and metalloid elements, e.g., Sn [,,,,]. The research on the oxidation of Nb-silicide-based alloys would suggest (a) that Ge and/or Sn are needed to suppress pest oxidation, and (b) that, when these alloying additions were present individually or simultaneously in the alloys, the spallation of their scales at high temperatures was not suppressed. It is now well established that Ge or Sn has an effect on macrosegregation and can also reduce the liquidus temperature of the alloy. Alloying with Sn can affect the stability of the Nbss but not the alloying with Ge, which can, however, significantly reduce the cracking of the substrate below the scale/substrate interface []. Unfortunately, from the oxidation research on multicomponent Nb-silicide-based alloys, it is not clear whether it was the synergy of Sn or Ge individually or simultaneously with Al, Cr, Si, and Ti that improved oxidation resistance, or whether the presence of oxygen scavenging Hf with/without transition and refractory metals and with some or all of the aforementioned elements was essential for increasing the oxidation resistance.
